technical.prompt: What is net capture for an exchange?
expectedPoints: Quoted per share (equities) or per contract (derivatives)

choices.answer: Fees charged minus rebates paid, per share traded

technical.prompt: What is an inverted or taker-maker venue?

choices.answer: A venue that charges makers and pays takers
distractors: A venue that pays both makers and takers
A venue that trades upside down
A venue with no fees at all

technical.prompt: What is tiered pricing on an exchange?

choices.answer: Fees that fall as a member's volume rises
distractors: A single fee for every member
Fees set by a government agency

technical.prompt: What is price-time priority?
expectedPoints: At same price, earliest order first

choices.answer: Best price first, then earliest order at that price
distractors: Newest order at a price fills first

technical.prompt: What is pro-rata matching?
expectedPoints: Fills shared by resting order size
Common in some futures and options

choices.answer: Sharing fills among resting orders by size
distractors: Filling the earliest order entirely first

technical.prompt: What is a limit order?
expectedPoints: Order to buy or sell at a set price or better
May not fill if the market never reaches that price
Rests on the book if it cannot fill immediately
A resting limit order provides liquidity

choices.answer: An order to trade at a set price or better
distractors: An order to trade at any price now
An order capped at one share
An order only for the close

technical.prompt: What is an iceberg order?
expectedPoints: Shows only part of total size

choices.answer: An order that displays only part of its size
distractors: An order for frozen food companies
An order that cancels when prices fall
An order hidden entirely from the book

technical.prompt: What is an immediate-or-cancel order?
expectedPoints: Fills what it can at once

choices.answer: It fills what it can at once and cancels the rest
distractors: It waits on the book all day
It must fill completely or not at all
It is only sent at the open

technical.prompt: What is an opening auction?

choices.answer: Collecting orders before the open to set one price
distractors: A sale of the exchange at the open
The first trade of the day only
A bidding war for new listings

technical.prompt: What is tick size?

choices.answer: The smallest price step a security can move
distractors: The number of trades per second
A fee for each price change

technical.prompt: What is a multilateral trading facility or alternative trading system?
expectedPoints: Non-exchange venue matching many buyers and sellers

choices.answer: A non-exchange venue matching many buyers and sellers
distractors: A single bank's internal trading desk
A venue for just one company's shares

technical.prompt: How does an all-to-all trading platform differ from a dealer-to-client one?
expectedPoints: Any participant can trade with any other

choices.answer: Anyone can trade with anyone, not just dealers
distractors: Only dealers may ever trade on it
It trades only a single bond
It has no electronic trading at all

technical.prompt: What is a systematic internaliser?
expectedPoints: Firm trading against clients on own account

choices.answer: A firm routinely filling client orders itself
distractors: A robot that runs an exchange
A firm that never trades at all

technical.prompt: Why do companies care which exchange they list on?

choices.answer: It shapes their investors, visibility and costs

technical.prompt: What is a speed bump?

choices.answer: A tiny deliberate delay blunting speed edges
distractors: A physical barrier on a trading floor
A limit on each member's daily volume
A rule halting trading over lunch

technical.prompt: What is a periodic auction?
expectedPoints: Frequent short auctions during the day

choices.answer: Frequent short auctions held throughout the day
distractors: A sale of old trading equipment

technical.prompt: Why do exchanges pay rebates to liquidity providers?

choices.answer: To attract resting orders that tighten spreads
distractors: To reward traders for losing money

technical.prompt: What is average daily volume?
expectedPoints: Average shares or contracts traded per day

choices.answer: The average amount traded per day
distractors: The price of the average share

technical.prompt: What is open interest?
expectedPoints: Number of futures or options contracts still open
Counts positions not yet closed out, offset or expired
Rises when new positions open and falls when they close
Signals participation and liquidity in a contract

choices.answer: Contracts still outstanding, not yet closed
distractors: Contracts traded in the last hour

technical.prompt: An exchange charges takers $0.0030 a share and pays makers $0.0020. If 1 billion shares match in a day, what is its net capture?

choices.answer: About $1 million

technical.prompt: Buy orders: 100 at $10.02, 200 at $10.01, 300 at $10.00. Sell orders: 250 at $9.99, 150 at $10.00, 200 at $10.01. At what price does the auction clear, and how many shares trade?

choices.answer: 400 shares at $10.00

technical.prompt: An exchange lists 3,000 companies paying an average annual fee of $100,000. What is its annual listing revenue?

choices.answer: About $300 million

technical.prompt: A derivatives exchange earns $0.60 per contract on 1.5 billion futures contracts and $0.30 per contract on 0.5 billion options contracts. What is its average revenue per contract?

choices.answer: About $0.525

technical.prompt: Industry volume is 12 billion shares a day. A venue has 15% market share and earns net capture of $0.0005 per share. What does it earn daily?
A stock trades at $2 with a one-cent tick. What is the minimum spread as a percentage?
A 100-lot order hits a price with resting orders of 300 and 200 lots under pro-rata matching. How is it filled?

choices.answer: 60 and 40 lots

technical.prompt: An exchange has 400,000 professional display users paying $50 a month for its data. What is its annual revenue from them?

choices.answer: About $240 million

technical.prompt: An exchange wins 200 IPOs in a year, each paying a $250,000 initial fee. What is its initial listing revenue, and why does it swing?

choices.answer: About $50 million, swinging with IPO markets

technical.prompt: Transaction fees are 60% of an exchange's revenue. If volumes fall 20% while fees per trade and all other revenue stay the same, roughly how much does total revenue fall?
expectedPoints: Non-transaction revenue such as data and listings cushions the fall

choices.answer: About 12%

technical.prompt: Why can a tick size that's too large hurt investors?

choices.answer: It forces wide spreads and pushes trades elsewhere
distractors: It has no effect on trading costs

technical.prompt: Why can a tick size that's too small hurt liquidity?

choices.answer: Queue-jumping thins displayed depth
distractors: It always deepens the order book

technical.prompt: Why might a trader route to an inverted venue even though it pays to post there?
expectedPoints: Takers are paid to trade there, so resting orders get hit sooner

choices.answer: Shorter queues mean faster fills
distractors: Inverted venues are always cheapest to post

technical.prompt: How does price-time priority shape trader behaviour?

choices.answer: It rewards speed, so traders race for position
distractors: It rewards only the largest orders
It fills orders in random order

technical.prompt: Why have periodic auctions grown in some markets?

choices.answer: They offer an alternative when dark trading is capped

technical.prompt: Why do bond markets rely more on request-for-quote than central order books?

choices.answer: Bonds are numerous and trade rarely
distractors: Bonds trade more often than stocks
Order books are illegal for bonds
There are very few bonds in issue

technical.prompt: How do exchanges compete for company listings?

choices.answer: Investor access, fees, index inclusion and rules
distractors: Only by offering the lowest fees

technical.prompt: What is the argument for speed bumps, and what is the criticism?
Why are derivatives exchanges often more profitable than equity exchanges?

choices.answer: Proprietary products, clearing and less fragmentation
distractors: They charge lower fees per contract
